 File names on Windows can also not end with the following characters. These only get replaced if they are the last character in the name: 

 <table> <tr VALIGN=top><td> Character </td><td ALIGN=center> Value </td><td ALIGN=center> Replacement 
</td></tr><tr VALIGN=top><td COLSPAN=3><hr></td></tr><tr VALIGN=top><td> SP </td><td ALIGN=center> 0x20 </td><td ALIGN=center> 20 
</td></tr><tr VALIGN=top><td> . </td><td ALIGN=center> 0x2E </td><td ALIGN=center> 0E 
</td></tr> </table> 

 Invalid UTF-8 bytes will also be replaced (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/overview/#invalid-utf8">https://rclone.org/overview/#invalid-utf8</a>), as they can't be converted to UTF-16.
<h3>Long paths on Windows</h3>Rclone handles long paths automatically, by converting all paths to long UNC paths (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa365247(v=vs.85).aspx#maxpath)">https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa365247(v=vs.85).aspx#maxpath)</a> which allows paths up to 32,767 characters. 

 This is why you will see that your paths, for instance c:\files is converted to the UNC path \\?\c:\files in the output, and \\server\share is converted to \\?\UNC\server\share. 

 However, in rare cases this may cause problems with buggy file system drivers like EncFS (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues/261">https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues/261</a>). To disable UNC conversion globally, add this to your .rclone.conf file:
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>[local]
nounc = true</pre></dl>
 

 If you want to selectively disable UNC, you can add it to a separate entry like this:
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>[nounc]
type = local
nounc = true</pre></dl>
 

 And use rclone like this: 

 rclone copy c:\src nounc:z:\dst 

 This will use UNC paths on c:\src but not on z:\dst. Of course this will cause problems if the absolute path length of a file exceeds 258 characters on z, so only use this option if you have to.
<h3>Symlinks / Junction points</h3>Normally rclone will ignore symlinks or junction points (which behave like symlinks under Windows). 

 If you supply --copy-links or -L then rclone will follow the symlink and copy the pointed to file or directory. Note that this flag is incompatible with -links / -l. 

 This flag applies to all commands. 

 For example, supposing you have a directory structure like this
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ tree /tmp/a
/tmp/a
1C0000 b -&gt; ../b
1C0000 expected -&gt; ../expected
1C0000 one
140000 two
 140000 three</pre></dl>
 

 Then you can see the difference with and without the flag like this
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone ls /tmp/a
 6 one
 6 two/three</pre></dl>
 

 and
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone -L ls /tmp/a
 4174 expected
 6 one
 6 two/three
 6 b/two
 6 b/one</pre></dl><h3>-links, -l</h3>Normally rclone will ignore symlinks or junction points (which behave like symlinks under Windows). 

 If you supply this flag then rclone will copy symbolic links from the local storage, and store them as text files, with a `.rclonelink' suffix in the remote storage. 

 The text file will contain the target of the symbolic link (see example). 

 This flag applies to all commands. 

 For example, supposing you have a directory structure like this
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ tree /tmp/a
/tmp/a
1C0000 file1 -&gt; ./file4
140000 file2 -&gt; /home/user/file3</pre></dl>
 

 Copying the entire directory with `-l'
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone copyto -l /tmp/a/file1 remote:/tmp/a/</pre></dl>
 

 The remote files are created with a `.rclonelink' suffix
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone ls remote:/tmp/a
 5 file1.rclonelink
 14 file2.rclonelink</pre></dl>
 

 The remote files will contain the target of the symbolic links
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone cat remote:/tmp/a/file1.rclonelink
./file4
$ rclone cat remote:/tmp/a/file2.rclonelink
/home/user/file3</pre></dl>
 

 Copying them back with `-l'
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone copyto -l remote:/tmp/a/ /tmp/b/
$ tree /tmp/b
/tmp/b
1C0000 file1 -&gt; ./file4
140000 file2 -&gt; /home/user/file3</pre></dl>
 

 However, if copied back without `-l'
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone copyto remote:/tmp/a/ /tmp/b/
$ tree /tmp/b
/tmp/b
1C0000 file1.rclonelink
140000 file2.rclonelink</pre></dl>
 

 Note that this flag is incompatible with -copy-links / -L.
<h3>Restricting filesystems with -one-file-system</h3>Normally rclone will recurse through filesystems as mounted. 

 However if you set --one-file-system or -x this tells rclone to stay in the filesystem specified by the root and not to recurse into different file systems. 

 For example if you have a directory hierarchy like this
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>root
1C0000 disk1 - disk1 mounted on the root
|&nbsp;<wbr>&nbsp; 140000 file3 - stored on disk1
1C0000 disk2 - disk2 mounted on the root
|&nbsp;<wbr>&nbsp; 140000 file4 - stored on disk12
1C0000 file1 - stored on the root disk
140000 file2 - stored on the root disk</pre></dl>
 

 Using rclone --one-file-system copy root remote: will only copy file1 and file2. Eg
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>$ rclone -q --one-file-system ls root
 0 file1
 0 file2</pre><dd><pre>$ rclone -q ls root
 0 disk1/file3
 0 disk2/file4
 0 file1
 0 file2</pre></dl>
 

 NB Rclone (like most unix tools such as du, rsync and tar) treats a bind mount to the same device as being on the same filesystem. 

 NB This flag is only available on Unix based systems. On systems where it isn't supported (eg Windows) it will be ignored.
<h3>Standard Options</h3>Here are the standard options specific to local (Local Disk).
<h3>-local-nounc</h3>Disable UNC (long path names) conversion on Windows
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: nounc
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_NOUNC
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: string
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: &quot;&quot;
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Examples:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>"true"
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Disables long file names</dl></dl>
</dl></dl>
</dl><h3>Advanced Options</h3>Here are the advanced options specific to local (Local Disk).
<h3>-copy-links / -L</h3>Follow symlinks and copy the pointed to item.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: copy_links
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_COPY_LINKS
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-links / -l</h3>Translate symlinks to/from regular files with a `.rclonelink' extension
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: links
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_LINKS
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-skip-links</h3>Don't warn about skipped symlinks. This flag disables warning messages on skipped symlinks or junction points, as you explicitly acknowledge that they should be skipped.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: skip_links
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_SKIP_LINKS
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-no-unicode-normalization</h3>Don't apply unicode normalization to paths and filenames (Deprecated) 

 This flag is deprecated now. Rclone no longer normalizes unicode file names, but it compares them with unicode normalization in the sync routine instead.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: no_unicode_normalization
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_NO_UNICODE_NORMALIZATION
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-no-check-updated</h3>Don't check to see if the files change during upload 

 Normally rclone checks the size and modification time of files as they are being uploaded and aborts with a message which starts "can't copy - source file is being updated" if the file changes during upload. 

 However on some file systems this modification time check may fail (eg Glusterfs #2206 (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues/2206))">https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues/2206))</a> so this check can be disabled with this flag. 

 If this flag is set, rclone will use its best efforts to transfer a file which is being updated. If the file is only having things appended to it (eg a log) then rclone will transfer the log file with the size it had the first time rclone saw it. 

 If the file is being modified throughout (not just appended to) then the transfer may fail with a hash check failure. 

 In detail, once the file has had stat() called on it for the first time we:
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Only transfer the size that stat gave
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Only checksum the size that stat gave
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Don't update the stat info for the file
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: no_check_updated
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_NO_CHECK_UPDATED
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-one-file-system / -x</h3>Don't cross filesystem boundaries (unix/macOS only).
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: one_file_system
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_ONE_FILE_SYSTEM
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-case-sensitive</h3>Force the filesystem to report itself as case sensitive. 

 Normally the local backend declares itself as case insensitive on Windows/macOS and case sensitive for everything else. Use this flag to override the default choice.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: case_sensitive
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_CASE_SENSITIVE
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-case-insensitive</h3>Force the filesystem to report itself as case insensitive 

 Normally the local backend declares itself as case insensitive on Windows/macOS and case sensitive for everything else. Use this flag to override the default choice.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: case_insensitive
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_CASE_INSENSITIVE
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-no-sparse</h3>Disable sparse files for multi-thread downloads 

 On Windows platforms rclone will make sparse files when doing multi-thread downloads. This avoids long pauses on large files where the OS zeros the file. However sparse files may be undesirable as they cause disk fragmentation and can be slow to work with.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: no_sparse
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_NO_SPARSE
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-no-set-modtime</h3>Disable setting modtime 

 Normally rclone updates modification time of files after they are done uploading. This can cause permissions issues on Linux platforms when the user rclone is running as does not own the file uploaded, such as when copying to a CIFS mount owned by another user. If this option is enabled, rclone will no longer update the modtime after copying a file.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: no_set_modtime
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_NO_SET_MODTIME
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: bool
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: false</dl><h3>-local-encoding</h3>This sets the encoding for the backend. 

 See: the encoding section in the overview (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/overview/#encoding)">https://rclone.org/overview/#encoding)</a> for more info.
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Config: encoding
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Env Var: RCLONE_LOCAL_ENCODING
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Type: MultiEncoder
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Default: Slash,Dot</dl><h3>Backend commands</h3>Here are the commands specific to the local backend. 

 Run them with
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>rclone backend COMMAND remote:</pre></dl>
 

 The help below will explain what arguments each command takes. 

 See the "rclone backend" command (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/commands/rclone_backend/)">https://rclone.org/commands/rclone_backend/)</a> for more info on how to pass options and arguments. 

 These can be run on a running backend using the rc command backend/command (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/rc/#backend/command">https://rclone.org/rc/#backend/command</a>).
<h3>noop</h3>A null operation for testing backend commands
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>rclone backend noop remote: [options] [&lt;arguments&gt;+]</pre></dl>
 

 This is a test command which has some options you can try to change the output. 

 Options:
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>"echo": echo the input arguments
<dt>&bull;
<dd>"error": return an error based on option value</dl><h2>Changelog</h2><h3>v1.53.3 - 2020-11-19</h3>See commits (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://github.com/rclone/rclone/compare/v1.53.2...v1.53.3)">https://github.com/rclone/rclone/compare/v1.53.2...v1.53.3)</a>

</dl><h3>v1.52.0 - 2020-05-27</h3>Special thanks to Martin Michlmayr for proof reading and correcting all the docs and Edward Barker for helping re-write the front page.

<dt>&bull;

<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

</dl><h3>v1.46 - 2019-02-09</h3><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

</dl><h3>v1.40 - 2018-03-19</h3><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>New backends
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;

<dd>New commands
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;

<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>by default this is a simple non recursive list of files and directories
<dt>&bull;
<dd>it can be configured to add more info in an easy to parse way</dl></dl><dt>&bull;
<dd>serve restic: for serving a remote as a Restic REST endpoint
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;
<dd>Thanks Alexander Neumann for help, patches and review</dl></dl><dt>&bull;
<dd>rc: enable the remote control of a running rclone
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>The running rclone must be started with -rc and related flags.
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Currently there is support for bwlimit, and flushing for mount and cache.</dl></dl>
</dl></dl><dt>&bull;
<dd>New Features

<dt>&bull;
<dd>cryptcheck: make reading of nonce more efficient with RangeOption</dl></dl><dt>&bull;
<dd>serve http/webdav/restic
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>support SSL/TLS
<dt>&bull;
<dd>add --user --pass and --htpasswd for authentication</dl></dl><dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;
<dd>lsjson: add --encrypted to show encrypted name (Jakub Tasiemski)
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Add --stats-file-name-length to specify the printed file name length for stats (Will Gunn)</dl></dl><dt>&bull;
<dd>Compile
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;
<dd>Add .deb and .rpm packages as part of the build
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Make a beta release for all branches on the main repo (but not pull requests)</dl></dl><dt>&bull;
<dd>Bug Fixes
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>config: fixes errors on non existing config by loading config file only on first access
<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<dt>&bull;

<h2>Bugs and Limitations</h2><a NAME="lb|T">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Limitations</h3><a NAME="lb|U">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Directory timestamps aren't preserved</h3>Rclone doesn't currently preserve the timestamps of directories. This is because rclone only really considers objects when syncing. <a NAME="lb|V">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Rclone struggles with millions of files in a directory/bucket</h3>Currently rclone loads each directory/bucket entirely into memory before using it. Since each rclone object takes 0.5k-1k of memory this can take a very long time and use a large amount of memory. 

 Millions of files in a directory tends to occur on bucket-based remotes (e.g. S3 buckets) since those remotes do not segregate subdirectories within the bucket. <a NAME="lb|W">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Bucket based remotes and folders</h3>Bucket based remotes (e.g. S3/GCS/Swift/B2) do not have a concept of directories. Rclone therefore cannot create directories in them which means that empty directories on a bucket based remote will tend to disappear. 

 Some software creates empty keys ending in / as directory markers. Rclone doesn't do this as it potentially creates more objects and costs more. This ability may be added in the future (probably via a flag/option). <a NAME="lb|X">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Bugs</h3>Bugs are stored in rclone's GitHub project:
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Reported bugs (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3Abug)">https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3Abug)</a>
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Known issues (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+milestone%3A%22Known+Problem%22)">https://github.com/rclone/rclone/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+milestone%3A%22Known+Problem%22)</a></dl>
 <a NAME="lb|Y">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Frequently Asked Questions</h3><a NAME="lb|Z">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Do all cloud storage systems support all rclone commands</h3>Yes they do. All the rclone commands (eg sync, copy etc) will work on all the remote storage systems. <a NAME="lb}A">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Can I copy the config from one machine to another</h3>Sure! Rclone stores all of its config in a single file. If you want to find this file, run rclone config file which will tell you where it is. 

 See the remote setup docs (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/remote_setup/)">https://rclone.org/remote_setup/)</a> for more info. <a NAME="lb}B">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>How do I configure rclone on a remote / headless box with no browser?</h3>This has now been documented in its own remote setup page (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/remote_setup/">https://rclone.org/remote_setup/</a>). <a NAME="lb}C">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Can rclone sync directly from drive to s3</h3>Rclone can sync between two remote cloud storage systems just fine. 

 Note that it effectively downloads the file and uploads it again, so the node running rclone would need to have lots of bandwidth. 

 The syncs would be incremental (on a file by file basis). 

 Eg
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>rclone sync -i drive:Folder s3:bucket</pre></dl>
 <a NAME="lb}D">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Using rclone from multiple locations at the same time</h3>You can use rclone from multiple places at the same time if you choose different subdirectory for the output, eg
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>Server A&gt; rclone sync -i /tmp/whatever remote:ServerA
Server B&gt; rclone sync -i /tmp/whatever remote:ServerB</pre></dl>
 

 If you sync to the same directory then you should use rclone copy otherwise the two instances of rclone may delete each other's files, eg
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>Server A&gt; rclone copy /tmp/whatever remote:Backup
Server B&gt; rclone copy /tmp/whatever remote:Backup</pre></dl>
 

 The file names you upload from Server A and Server B should be different in this case, otherwise some file systems (eg Drive) may make duplicates. <a NAME="lb}E">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Why doesn't rclone support partial transfers / binary diffs like rsync?</h3>Rclone stores each file you transfer as a native object on the remote cloud storage system. This means that you can see the files you upload as expected using alternative access methods (eg using the Google Drive web interface). There is a 1:1 mapping between files on your hard disk and objects created in the cloud storage system. 

 Cloud storage systems (at least none I've come across yet) don't support partially uploading an object. You can't take an existing object, and change some bytes in the middle of it. 

 It would be possible to make a sync system which stored binary diffs instead of whole objects like rclone does, but that would break the 1:1 mapping of files on your hard disk to objects in the remote cloud storage system. 

 All the cloud storage systems support partial downloads of content, so it would be possible to make partial downloads work. However to make this work efficiently this would require storing a significant amount of metadata, which breaks the desired 1:1 mapping of files to objects. <a NAME="lb}F">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Can rclone do bi-directional sync?</h3>No, not at present. rclone only does uni-directional sync from A -&gt; B. It may do in the future though since it has all the primitives - it just requires writing the algorithm to do it. <a NAME="lb}G">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Can I use rclone with an HTTP proxy?</h3>Yes. rclone will follow the standard environment variables for proxies, similar to cURL and other programs. 

 In general the variables are called http_proxy (for services reached over http) and https_proxy (for services reached over https). Most public services will be using https, but you may wish to set both. 

 The content of the variable is protocol://server:port. The protocol value is the one used to talk to the proxy server, itself, and is commonly either http or socks5. 

 Slightly annoyingly, there is no standard for the name; some applications may use http_proxy but another one HTTP_PROXY. The Go libraries used by rclone will try both variations, but you may wish to set all possibilities. So, on Linux, you may end up with code similar to
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>export http_proxy=<a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://proxyserver:12345">http://proxyserver:12345</a>
export https_proxy=$http_proxy
export HTTP_PROXY=$http_proxy
export HTTPS_PROXY=$http_proxy</pre></dl>
 

 The NO_PROXY allows you to disable the proxy for specific hosts. Hosts must be comma separated, and can contain domains or parts. For instance "foo.com" also matches "bar.foo.com". 

 e.g.
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>export no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.0/8,my.host.name
export NO_PROXY=$no_proxy</pre></dl>
 

 Note that the ftp backend does not support ftp_proxy yet. <a NAME="lb}H">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Rclone gives x509: failed to load system roots and no roots provided error</h3>This means that rclone can't file the SSL root certificates. Likely you are running rclone on a NAS with a cut-down Linux OS, or possibly on Solaris. 

 Rclone (via the Go runtime) tries to load the root certificates from these places on Linux.
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>&quot;/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt&quot;, // Debian/Ubuntu/Gentoo etc.
&quot;/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt&quot;, // Fedora/RHEL
&quot;/etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem&quot;, // OpenSUSE
&quot;/etc/pki/tls/cacert.pem&quot;, // OpenELEC</pre></dl>
 

 So doing something like this should fix the problem. It also sets the time which is important for SSL to work properly.
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>mkdir -p /etc/ssl/certs/
curl -o /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt <a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bagder/ca-bundle/master/ca-bundle.crt">https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bagder/ca-bundle/master/ca-bundle.crt</a>
ntpclient -s -h pool.ntp.org</pre></dl>
 

 The two environment variables SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR, mentioned in the x509 package (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://godoc.org/crypto/x509">https://godoc.org/crypto/x509</a>), provide an additional way to provide the SSL root certificates. 

 Note that you may need to add the --insecure option to the curl command line if it doesn't work without.
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre>curl --insecure -o /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt <a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bagder/ca-bundle/master/ca-bundle.crt">https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bagder/ca-bundle/master/ca-bundle.crt</a></pre></dl>
 <a NAME="lb}I">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Rclone gives Failed to load config file: function not implemented error</h3>Likely this means that you are running rclone on Linux version not supported by the go runtime, ie earlier than version 2.6.23. 

 See the system requirements section in the go install docs (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://golang.org/doc/install)">https://golang.org/doc/install)</a> for full details. <a NAME="lb}J">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>All my uploaded docx/xlsx/pptx files appear as archive/zip</h3>This is caused by uploading these files from a Windows computer which hasn't got the Microsoft Office suite installed. The easiest way to fix is to install the Word viewer and the Microsoft Office Compatibility Pack for Word, Excel, and PowerPoint 2007 and later versions' file formats <a NAME="lb}K">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>tcp lookup some.domain.com no such host</h3>This happens when rclone cannot resolve a domain. Please check that your DNS setup is generally working, e.g.
<dl COMPACT><dd><pre># both should print a long list of possible IP addresses
dig <a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://www.googleapis.com">www.googleapis.com</a> # resolve using your default DNS
dig <a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://www.googleapis.com">www.googleapis.com</a> @8.8.8.8 # resolve with Google's DNS server</pre></dl>
 

 If you are using systemd-resolved (default on Arch Linux), ensure it is at version 233 or higher. Previous releases contain a bug which causes not all domains to be resolved properly. 

 Additionally with the GODEBUG=netdns= environment variable the Go resolver decision can be influenced. This also allows to resolve certain issues with DNS resolution. See the name resolution section in the go docs (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://golang.org/pkg/net/#hdr-Name_Resolution">https://golang.org/pkg/net/#hdr-Name_Resolution</a>). <a NAME="lb}L">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>The total size reported in the stats for a sync is wrong and keeps changing</h3>It is likely you have more than 10,000 files that need to be synced. By default rclone only gets 10,000 files ahead in a sync so as not to use up too much memory. You can change this default with the -max-backlog (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://rclone.org/docs/#max-backlog-n)">https://rclone.org/docs/#max-backlog-n)</a> flag. <a NAME="lb}M">&nbsp;</a>
<h3>Rclone is using too much memory or appears to have a memory leak</h3>Rclone is written in Go which uses a garbage collector. The default settings for the garbage collector mean that it runs when the heap size has doubled. 

 However it is possible to tune the garbage collector to use less memory by setting GOGC (<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://dave.cheney.net/tag/gogc)">https://dave.cheney.net/tag/gogc)</a> to a lower value, say export GOGC=20. This will make the garbage collector work harder, reducing memory size at the expense of CPU usage. 

 The most common cause of rclone using lots of memory is a single directory with thousands or millions of files in. Rclone has to load this entirely into memory as rclone objects. Each rclone object takes 0.5k-1k of memory. <a NAME="lb}N">&nbsp;</a>
